Al-Biruni: Scholar of the 11th Century

Al-Biruni, also written Alberuni, was a scholar from Khwarizm in present-day Uzbekistan. He was born in 973 CE and was knowledgeable in several languages and subjects, including mathematics, astronomy and the study of religious and philosophical traditions.

He became associated with the Ghaznavid world during the time of Mahmud of Ghazni. Following Mahmud's conquest of Khwarizm in 1017, Al-Biruni was taken to Ghazni, where his interest in India developed further.

Al-Biruni studied Sanskrit and interacted with Indian scholars. He used Indian texts to learn about religious beliefs, philosophical ideas, sciences and social practices.

His exact itinerary in India is not fully established. It is therefore better to associate him securely with the study of India, particularly northern India, than to assume he visited every region described in his writings.

The Kitab-ul-Hind

Al-Biruni's famous work is the Kitab-ul-Hind, written in Arabic. It presents a broad study of Indian knowledge and society.

The work contains 80 chapters dealing with subjects such as:

  • Religion and philosophy: Indian beliefs, sacred texts and philosophical ideas.
  • Social organisation: customs and descriptions of social divisions, including caste.
  • Science: astronomy, mathematical knowledge and related intellectual traditions.
  • Everyday practices: festivals, customs, weights, measures and other aspects of life.

Al-Biruni frequently explained Indian ideas with reference to Sanskrit learning and compared them with knowledge familiar to readers from other cultural traditions.

His work is therefore distinct from the religious travel accounts of the Chinese Buddhist pilgrims. Although he studied Indian religions, his purpose was not simply to visit Buddhist pilgrimage centres or collect Buddhist monastic rules.

Al-Biruni and his work: 11th century CE; Khwarizm and the Ghaznavid period; Sanskrit learning; Kitab-ul-Hind in Arabic; Indian religion, philosophy, society, mathematics and astronomy.

Identify the 5 Travellers by Period, Work and Main Interest

TravellerPeriod and settingWork and main observations
MegasthenesLate 4th to early 3rd century BCE; Chandragupta MauryaIndica; Mauryan court, administration and society
FaxianEarly 5th century CE; Gupta periodA Record of Buddhist Kingdoms; Buddhist sites, manuscripts and social conditions
Xuanzang7th century CE; HarshavardhanaGreat Tang Records on the Western Regions; kingdoms, Buddhist sites and Nalanda
YijingLater 7th century CEA Record of the Buddhist Religion as Practised in India and the Malay Archipelago; monastic discipline and learning
Al-Biruni11th century CE; Ghaznavid periodKitab-ul-Hind; religion, philosophy, society and sciences

The first useful distinction is chronology: Megasthenes belongs to the Mauryan period, Faxian to the Gupta period, Xuanzang and Yijing to the 7th century, and Al-Biruni to the 11th century.

The second distinction is purpose: Megasthenes was a Greek diplomat; Faxian, Xuanzang and Yijing were Chinese Buddhist monks; Al-Biruni was a scholar investigating Indian knowledge and society.

Identify the 4 Educational Centres by Location and Patronage

CentrePresent-day locationHistorical associationImportant learning
TaxilaPunjab, PakistanAncient Gandhara; independent teachers; no single securely established royal founderScriptures, law, medicine, astronomy, military science
NalandaNalanda district, BiharGupta beginnings associated with Kumaragupta I; later Harsha and Pala supportBuddhist philosophy, logic, grammar, medicine, mathematics, astronomy
VallabhiSaurashtra, GujaratMaitraka rulers and other donorsBuddhist learning, logic, grammar, literature and law
VikramashilaBhagalpur district, BiharFounded under the Pala ruler DharmapalaBuddhist philosophy, logic, grammar and Vajrayana studies

Connect the Institutions with the Travellers

Not every foreign traveller was connected to every educational institution. The most important supported relationships are:

  • Xuanzang and Nalanda: he studied there under Shilabhadra and described its learned community.
  • Xuanzang and Vallabhi: he visited the city and described its Buddhist institutions.
  • Yijing and Nalanda: he studied there and recorded monastic practices.
  • Yijing and Vallabhi: he recognised its educational reputation alongside Nalanda; a personal visit should not be assumed from that statement.

By contrast, Megasthenes is primarily associated with the Mauryan court, Faxian with Buddhist pilgrimage in the Gupta age, and Al-Biruni with the study of Indian intellectual and social traditions in the 11th century.

Reasoning with Dates, Places and Patrons

Statement-based prelims questions can be approached by checking 3 relationships: when a person or institution belonged, where an institution was located, and who supported or described it.

For example, the claim that Xuanzang studied at Nalanda during Harsha's period is chronologically consistent. The claim that he studied at Vikramashila under Dharmapala would be incorrect because Vikramashila was founded later, in the Pala period.

Similarly, identifying Vallabhi as a centre of Maitraka Gujarat is correct, while placing it in Bihar would confuse it with Nalanda or Vikramashila.

Correct historical matching depends on maintaining these distinctions rather than memorising names in isolation.

Prelims focus

  • Indica is associated with Megasthenes and the Mauryan period.
  • A Record of Buddhist Kingdoms is associated with Faxian and the Gupta age.
  • Xuanzang and Yijing are 7th-century Chinese Buddhist travellers associated with Nalanda.
  • Kitab-ul-Hind was written in Arabic by Al-Biruni.
  • Taxila was in Gandhara; Vallabhi was in Gujarat; Nalanda and Vikramashila were in Bihar.
  • Trap: Kumaragupta I is associated with Nalanda's early foundation, while Dharmapala is associated with the foundation of Vikramashila.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Class 12, Theme 5, 'Through the Eyes of Travellers', sections 'Al-Biruni and the Kitab-ul-Hind' and 'Making Sense of an Alien World', printed pp. 116–117 and 124 onward; NCERT, It So Happened, Class 8, chapter 'Ancient Education System of India', pp. 69–73, 2024–25 reprint; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, printed pp. 32–34; NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class 6, chapter 'Traders, Kings and Pilgrims', printed pp. 105–106, 2018–19 edition; Annette Schmiedchen, 'Maitrakas', Encyclopedia of Ancient History: Asia and Africa, 2021; Archaeological Survey of India, Patna Circle, entry on Vikramashila; online sources consulted 18 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Timeline of four educational centres and five travellers, distinguishing study from place observations and flagging impossible chronological matches.
pictures.caption: The chronology of institutions and travellers explains which historical connections are possible.

title: Al-Biruni and the Essential Comparison of Ancient Universities and Travellers
